title: A Pentecostal service
hookLine: long praise, open prayer, testimony, altar call

lines: THE ROOM IS ALREADY ON ITS FEET.
cards: The drummer counts in, and the room is already on its feet. A song starts and keeps going, the same chorus again and again, louder, then softer, then louder. Hands go up all over the room.
A woman near the front is crying, and smiling. Somebody shouts amen in the middle of a line.

Then the pastor says, let's pray, and the whole room prays out loud at once, every voice saying something different, a wave of sound. Yesterday's room waited in silence. This one waits with everything it's got.

teach.h: A ROOM, A WIND, AND OTHER TONGUES.
teach.b: Pentecostal churches take their name from a day in the book of Acts. The followers of Jesus are together in one place.
"And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting."
Then "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Pentecostals expect that same Spirit in the room today.
First, long praise: not one hymn but a stretch of singing, often with hands raised, sometimes with dancing. A psalm gives the reason: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD."
Second, open prayer: many voices praying aloud together, and some praying in tongues, a prayer language they understand as a gift of the Spirit.
Other Christians understand the gift of tongues differently, and some believe it belonged to the earliest church. Pentecostals hold that it's for now. Third, testimony.
Someone stands and tells what God has done for them this week: a healing, a job, a night they didn't drink. Ordinary people with a microphone, telling the truth.
Fourth, the altar call. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who wants prayer, or wants to give their life to Christ, to come to the front, and others gather round, lay hands on them and pray.

Behind it all stands a line Jesus said to Nicodemus: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit."
Wind you can hear, but can't hold.

how: Pentecostal and charismatic churches typically hold long times of sung praise with raised hands, open prayer in which some pray in tongues, testimonies from members and an altar call inviting people forward for prayer.

o: a quiet service of chanted psalms in an old church
a service held only on the feast of Pentecost each year
worship that expects the Spirit to move in the room

games.q: you're one of Jesus's followers, all together in one place. suddenly there's a sound like a rushing mighty wind, filling the house. what happens next?
o: everyone runs outside to see the storm.
they're filled with the Holy Ghost and speak with other tongues.
nothing; it passes, and they go home.
games.why: "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."

practice: If you can, play a song of praise from any church you like; if not, hum, or breathe out slowly a few times. Let your body join in somehow, hands open on your knees or lifted a little, whatever feels honest.
If you pray, thank God out loud for one thing; if not, say aloud one thing you're glad of today.

wordCard.voice: A Pentecostal service. Worship named for the day of Pentecost, expecting the Spirit to move in the room.

orig.note: Greek: wind, breath, spirit — John 3:8 plays on it, so the wind that blows and the Spirit are one word.

carryVoice: Your line: the spirit moves. Everything that has breath gets to join in. Same time tomorrow.
